messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Karim's Story

Karim was thirty-eight when the diagnosis came back positive. The oncologist had used words like "aggressive" and "chemotherapy," and Karim had sat in that examination room feeling his body betray him in real time—his heart accelerating, his palms sweating, the fluorescent lights suddenly too bright. The months that followed were a blur of hospital visits, infusions that burned through his veins, and nights when he lay awake convinced he could feel the cancer spreading despite what the scans said. He'd lost his hair during treatment, watched it fall in clumps into the shower drain, and by the time remission came nine months later, something fundamental had shifted inside him. The cancer was gone. Karim was alive. But his body had become a stranger.

Now, three years into remission, Karim worked as a hairdresser in a busy salon in Arlington, a job that had always grounded him—the ritual of it, the trust clients placed in his hands, the simple geometry of making someone feel better about themselves. But everything had changed. Photographs triggered him without warning. A client would show him a picture of a hairstyle she wanted, and the image would pull something loose in his chest. He couldn't explain why. Sometimes it was just the color in the photo—a particular shade of grey that reminded him of the hospital walls—and suddenly his body was flooded with the same dread he'd felt waiting for biopsy results. His hands would shake as he held the scissors. When he woke from nightmares—and he woke from them most nights, drenched in sweat, his heart hammering—the residual fear would linger through his entire shift, making him hypervigilant, certain that something was wrong with him again, though he couldn't articulate what.

Medical procedures were the worst. When his dentist had needed to do a routine cleaning last month, Karim had felt his entire body lock into a state of red alert before the appointment even began. The moment the hygienist leaned in with her instruments, he could smell the antiseptic—and suddenly he wasn't in a dental chair but in the oncology ward, the chemical smell of the infusion center flooding his nostrils, his body remembering the nausea, the bone-deep ache that had accompanied each treatment. His muscles tensed so violently he nearly jumped out of the chair. The physical reactivity was involuntary, humiliating. His body was treating a simple cleaning as a mortal threat.

What frightened Karim most was the conviction that had crystallized in his mind over these three years: his body could no longer be trusted. It had already tried to kill him once. Now it was overreacting to everything, sending false alarms, making him feel constantly tense and ready to react to danger even when he was sitting safely in his apartment on a Sunday afternoon. He had come to believe that these reactions meant something was fundamentally broken inside him. The intensity of his fear, the way it could arrive without any clear trigger, the physical sensations that mimicked his illness—all of it convinced him he was going crazy. If a normal person could sit through a dental appointment without their body screaming in terror, what did it say about him that he couldn't? The more he tried to suppress these thoughts, the more they cycled back. His body felt like an enemy that had learned to disguise its attacks as ordinary moments.

The negative appraisals had become self-perpetuating. Because he believed his body was unreliable and dangerous, he began to scrutinize every sensation—a flutter in his chest became a sign of recurrence, a headache a harbinger of something worse. This hypervigilance fed the threat response, which in turn triggered fragmented memories: the smell of the IV port, the phantom pain in his arms where the catheters had been placed, the overwhelming dread that sometimes arrived without any image at all, just the raw emotional intensity of those nine months compressed into a moment. And these memories, once activated, would make him avoid the very situations that had triggered them—he'd stopped going to the doctor for routine checkups, had nearly lost a regular client rather than look at her wedding photos, had started making excuses to leave the salon when certain smells wafted in from the street. Each avoidance reinforced the belief that these situations were genuinely dangerous, that his body's fear response was justified, that something was still deeply wrong.

It was his sister who finally insisted he see someone. She'd noticed him becoming smaller, more isolated, the light draining from his eyes. Karim had resisted, convinced that no therapist could fix a body that had already proven itself capable of betrayal. But he was tired—tired of the nightmares, tired of his body's constant vigilance, tired of the shame that accompanied each panic response. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to articulate it, was the possibility that his body might someday feel like his own again.
